newsitem.title: USA: IMF sees stronger world economy in 1997.
newsitem.headline: IMF sees stronger world economy in 1997.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund's policy-making Interim Committee on Sunday welcomed the recent improvement in the world economy and saw prospects for a stronger and broader expansion into 1997.

In a communique and a declaration issued after a day of talks, the committee also endorsed a multibillion-dollar plan to provide relief to debt-strapped poor nations, but it did not specify where all the financing would come from.
While pledging to find the funds, the panel sidestepped a controversial issue of whether to sell off some of the Fund's gold for that purpose.

The IMF panel gave a variety of reasons for expecting better economic times ahead, including progress toward price stability, improvement in currency market conditions, rapid growth of trade and lower budget deficits.
It called inflation in industrial countries "subdued."

"Japan's recovery is more firmly established," the panel added. "In continental Western Europe, the standstill in growth has ended and conditions are now in place for a resumption of more satisfactory growth."
The committee, meeting during the annual IMF/World Bank gathering, stressed the importance of sound macroeconomic policies and the avoidance of large trade imbalances to avert currency misalignments.
It also highlighted the need for its member nations to eliminate budget deficits in the medium term.

"Continued fiscal imbalances and excessive public indebtedness, and the upward pressures they put on global real interest rates, are threats to financial stability and durable growth," the committee said.
